Al-Maʾmūn himself was determined that this policy should not collapse after his death. In his final instructions to al-Muʿtaṣim he wrote: “Follow your brother’s course regarding the Qurʾān.” He meant, of course, the Muʿtazilite doctrine that the Qurʾān was created.

The Muʿtazilite school was able to remain the official doctrine of the state under both al-Muʿtaṣim and al-Wāthiq because the conditions we have just described were still in place. In other words, the social forces that had supported al-Maʾmūn remained close to the center of power until the end of al-Wāthiq’s reign.
Under al-Mutawakkil, however, these forces were pushed aside and replaced by others that supported conservative thought, as we will soon see.
We have already seen a revolutionary side to Muʿtazilite kalām. It appeared in the method itself, especially in its rationalist character.
But this should not make us overlook its other side.
Muʿtazilite kalām still remained within the wider framework of official theological ideology. It did not break free of that framework.

Muʿtazilite thought was based on the principle of the absolute transcendence of the divine essence. This was the “official” understanding of divine unity. It also implied that truth itself was one. That truth was religious truth: the divine law, the sharia, which came from a single divine source.
This was the ideological foundation of the ruling class in the Islamic caliphate.
Because the caliphal state presented itself as the state of Islam, it also presented itself as the sole legitimate representative of the social order defined by divine law.
From this comes a line of reasoning that provides an Islamic “theoretical” basis for the idea of a divine right to absolute rule.
It can be set out as follows.
First, the social order approved by the sharia is the same order embodied by the caliphal state.
Second, the sharia that approves this order is divine, and therefore sacred.
The “logical” conclusion is that the political order of the caliphate is itself sacred.
Once the rule of the caliphal state is given a religiously sacred character, the ruling class gains a claim to absolute authority.
Opposition to that authority, disobedience to it, and especially rebellion against it can then be treated, within the law of the ruling system, as nothing more than religious heresy.
To oppose the state becomes opposition to God’s rule. To disobey it becomes disobedience to the “holder of authority,” whose obedience God is said to have commanded.
And if this is true even of ordinary opposition, what then of open revolt?
Whether the Muʿtazilites wanted this conclusion or not, and whether they consciously thought it through or not, is beside the point.

The issue does not depend on their wishes or intentions. Nor does it depend on whether this interpretation of Muʿtazilite thought is correct in some final or absolute sense. That is not the question we are trying to settle here.
Our concern is with the ideological meaning of Muʿtazilite kalām and with the relationship between that meaning and the ideology of the existing caliphal state.
If we look at Muʿtazilite kalām through its rationalist method, it was progressive in relation to its historical setting.
If we look at its ideological content, however, it supported that ruling ideology and gave it a “theoretical” foundation.

Even so, the rationalist method remained the dominant and genuinely new feature of Muʿtazilite kalām. Its progressive side was still the stronger one, because it dealt a damaging blow to the traditionalist ideology of its time.
B — The Ashʿarite Stage of Kalām
A traditionalist turn came after the death of al-Wāthiq.

Al-Wāthiq had refused to pass the Abbasid caliphate to his son Muḥammad. This gave his brother al-Mutawakkil the opportunity to become caliph in 232 AH/847 CE, with the support of forces hostile to the positive gains that had been made since the time of al-Maʾmūn.

One of the greatest of those gains, in terms of its importance for civilization and for social and scientific development, was the movement that translated the sciences into Arabic and brought them into Arab-Islamic intellectual life and society.
But that movement had grown out of the objective development and objective needs of society. It was not simply the product of the will of one ruler or one ruling group.
For that reason, no individual and no opposing movement could simply destroy it and take away what society had gained from it.
As one modern scholar puts it, al-Mutawakkil happened to be “the first of the Abbasid caliphs to surpass his predecessors in his love of luxury.”

The feudal landholders, the inner court circle, and their conservative intellectual representatives took advantage of this weakness in al-Mutawakkil’s character. They became a source of pressure on him and pushed his policies toward their own interests and outlook.
Muʿtazilite kalām, and especially the doctrine of the created Qurʾān, had been tied to the official doctrine of the state since 218 AH, when al-Maʾmūn formally declared this connection.
The dominant forces under al-Mutawakkil made this one of their main targets. They wanted to undo what al-Maʾmūn had established.
Al-Mutawakkil finally abolished it in 234 AH, only two years after becoming caliph.
The conservative forces celebrated this so strongly that they placed al-Mutawakkil alongside the first Rightly Guided Caliph, Abū Bakr, and the Umayyad caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.
“Three caliphs stand above the rest: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq on the day of the apostasy wars, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz when he restored people’s rights, and al-Mutawakkil when he revived the Sunna.”

We should also say here that the persecution directed against the opponents of the Muʿtazilites and of the doctrine of the created Qurʾān under al-Maʾmūn, al-Muʿtaṣim, and al-Wāthiq ultimately helped those opponents more than it helped the Muʿtazilites themselves.

The conservatives made full use of this persecution in shaping public opinion. They then used it as both an argument and a justification for the persecution that was later turned against the Muʿtazilites and their school for a long period afterward.
For this reason, we see the original campaign of persecution as a historical mistake.

It helped the conservative forces of the period launch a powerful reaction that brought the Muʿtazilite stage of kalām to an end before it had exhausted its possibilities and before it had completed its historical role in the development of Arab thought toward philosophy and the natural sciences.
The direction taken by the rationalist tendency within Muʿtazilite kalām now changed.
Kalām began to move into its second major stage.

About half a century after the end of the Muʿtazilite period, this new stage would be led by a major Sunni thinker who created the first new theoretical formulation of the ideology of the conservative forces. This ideology would later become the official ideology of state power for several generations.
We mean Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī (260–330 AH/873–941 CE).
This is why the period came to bear al-Ashʿarī’s name, even though it had begun quite some time before him.

Before al-Ashʿarī, it had already been led by al-Ḥārith ibn Asad al-Muḥāsibī, who died in 243 AH/857 CE, and by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd ibn Kullāb. They were the first founders, after the defeat of the Muʿtazilites, of a school that based itself on the texts of the Qurʾān and Sunna alone and openly declared a doctrinal war against Muʿtazilite thought.

How, then, should we understand the strength of the Ashʿarite school and the dominance it achieved from the end of the third Islamic century—the ninth century CE—not only over kalām, but over Sunni Islamic thought more generally?
We cannot understand the answer without looking at the method al-Ashʿarī used when he returned to the doctrine of the early hadith scholars.
There was nothing new about relying in theory on Sunni teaching in questions of religion, society, and nature.
What was new, and what gave Ashʿarism its special importance, was the method al-Ashʿarī used.
That method gave his school enough strength to justify its continued existence after Muʿtazilism had disappeared from the main arena of kalām.

If we look at the substance of the matter rather than its surface appearance, and if we do not concern ourselves with personal intentions or wishes, it becomes easy to see a kind of continuation of the Muʿtazilite method within the Ashʿarite method itself.

The rationalist direction that the Muʿtazilites had established in Arab thought, and had made the foundation of kalām from the moment they first shaped it as a discipline, could not simply be extinguished by the conservative wave that removed them from direct influence over intellectual development.

Nor could that conservative wave build a strong enough barrier to prevent Muʿtazilite rationalism from continuing to influence intellectual development indirectly, despite the severe repression directed against free thought and independent thinkers.

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī could not return to the doctrine of the Sunnis without carrying with him the results of the historical process that had given Arab thought as a whole—including kalām—a rationalist direction.
The Muʿtazilites had led that process from the late seventh century, throughout the eighth century, and into the first third of the ninth century CE.
It was therefore natural that when al-Ashʿarī entered the intellectual battlefield to fight Muʿtazilite thought, he appeared armed with the Muʿtazilites’ own weapon: the weapon of rational method.
But, as we will soon see, he changed that method in a fundamental way. The change stripped it of its original meaning and emptied it of its essential rationalism.
It might be argued that al-Ashʿarī’s commitment to rational method, even if only at the level of form, came from his own intellectual background.
After all, he had been trained in kalām by the Muʿtazilites. He studied under one of their leading teachers in Basra, Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī, who died in 303 AH/915 CE.

Al-Ashʿarī remained a Muʿtazilite until around 300 AH, when he broke with them. From the pulpit of a mosque in Basra, he publicly announced that he had repented and abandoned the positions in which he had followed the Muʿtazilites. He declared that he would now refute them and expose their “scandals.”

Even so, we do not think his Muʿtazilite upbringing is enough to explain why a rationalist method, in some form, appeared in Ashʿarite kalām and continued among later Ashʿarite thinkers, from Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī to al-Ghazālī and beyond.
There are two reasons for this.
First, al-Ashʿarī was a major thinker who was highly conscious of what he was doing. He made a serious effort to watch for the continued influence of his Muʿtazilite period on his later thinking.
He did this so that the “holy” war he had declared against Muʿtazilism could be carried through without compromise.
Second, if his Muʿtazilite upbringing were really the main reason for the appearance of rational method in Ashʿarism, we would expect that feature to disappear among his followers.

Some of the greatest Ashʿarite theologians after Abū al-Ḥasan developed the method further. They introduced new questions into their theology that had more in common with this rational method than with the methods of the Sunnis before the rise of the Muʿtazilites.

One example is the judge Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī, who died in 403 AH/1012 CE. He “developed the method and laid down the rational premises on which proof and inquiry depend, including such matters as establishing the indivisible atom, the void, the principle that one accident cannot inhere in another accident, and the principle that an accident does not remain for two moments.”

For all these reasons, we argue that when al-Ashʿarī used the outward forms of rational method in his theological school against Muʿtazilite kalām, he understood that his age no longer allowed Muʿtazilite thought to be fought with an entirely different kind of thought.
A purely traditionalist method had already been left behind by the historical process.
The same is entirely true of al-Ghazālī when he later declared his own ideological “holy war” against philosophical thought that had moved beyond traditional theology.

This is why we find Ashʿarite kalām using logical argument, speaking in the language of the authority of reason, refusing to openly accept absolute determinism in the question of human action, and discussing substance and accident, atomism, and even causation.
This is the general structure of the Ashʿarite method.

It gives the appearance of being “rationalist” because it needed a justification for its own existence in an age when Muʿtazilite rationalism had already established both direct and indirect influence.
But what was the real value of this Ashʿarite “rationalism”?
1 — It is true that al-Ashʿarī did not abandon logical argument.
But rationalism does not consist simply in the formal use of logic. It also depends on the rational starting points from which the premises of an argument are drawn.
For the Ashʿarites, all those starting points were confined to the content of religious texts, and nothing else.
2 — It is also true that they refer to reason when discussing the existence of God, the creation or beginning of the world, or the eternity of the divine attributes.
But according to the basic principles of their school, reason is not the true source of knowledge.
Reason cannot by itself decide what is good or bad in things, actions, values, or meanings.
They hold that knowledge of God can be reached through reason, but that revelation is what makes belief in God binding.
In other words, knowledge reached by reason is not enough to create religious obligation or responsibility.
Reason therefore plays only a secondary and guiding role.
The final authority is divine revelation.
3 — It is also true that the Ashʿarites rejected the strict determinist position that God creates human actions in an absolute sense.
But what did their own position really amount to?
